questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $p$ and $q$ are two statements, show that $p \Rightarrow q$ is logically equivalent to $\sim(p \wedge \sim q)$. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Truth table.**

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \Rightarrow q$ | $\sim q$ | $p \wedge \sim q$ | $\sim(p \wedge \sim q)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | F | F | T |
| T | F | F | T | T | F |
| F | T | T | F | F | T |
| F | F | T | T | F | T |

The columns of $p \Rightarrow q$ and of $\sim(p \wedge \sim q)$ are identical in every row, so the two statements are logically equivalent. $\blacksquare$

**Algebraic check.** By De Morgan's law and the double negation law,

$$\sim(p \wedge \sim q) \equiv \sim p \vee \sim(\sim q) \equiv \sim p \vee q,$$

and $p \Rightarrow q \equiv \sim p \vee q$ (a conditional is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false).

questions.enonce_markdown: The function $f: \mathbb{R} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is given by $f(x) = 2x^3 + 3x - 2$. Show that $f$ is monotonic increasing. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Differentiate:

$$f'(x) = 6x^2 + 3.$$

Since $x^2 \geq 0$ for every real $x$, we have $f'(x) = 6x^2 + 3 \geq 3 > 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. A function whose derivative is positive on all of $\mathbb{R}$ is (strictly) increasing there: for $x_1 < x_2$, $f(x_1) < f(x_2)$. Hence $f$ is monotonic increasing. $\blacksquare$

questions.enonce_markdown: The function $f: \mathbb{R} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is given by $f(x) = 2x^3 + 3x - 2$. Deduce that the equation $f(x) = 0$ has a root within the interval $0 < x < 1$. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
$f$ is a polynomial, hence continuous on $[0, 1]$. Evaluate at the ends of the interval:

$$f(0) = -2 < 0, \qquad f(1) = 2 + 3 - 2 = 3 > 0.$$

$f(0)$ and $f(1)$ have opposite signs, so by the intermediate value theorem there is a value $x$ with $0 < x < 1$ such that $f(x) = 0$.

Because $f$ is increasing (part (a)), this root is the only real root of the equation. $\blacksquare$

questions.enonce_markdown: Taking $x = 0.5$ as first approximation to the root of the equation $f(x) = 0$, where $f(x) = 2x^3 + 3x - 2$, use Newton-Raphson's method once to obtain, to $2$ decimal places, a second approximation to the root of this equation. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Newton-Raphson iteration: $x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$, with $f(x) = 2x^3 + 3x - 2$ and $f'(x) = 6x^2 + 3$.

At $x_0 = 0.5$:

$$f(0.5) = 2(0.125) + 1.5 - 2 = -0.25, \qquad f'(0.5) = 6(0.25) + 3 = 4.5.$$

$$x_1 = 0.5 - \frac{-0.25}{4.5} = 0.5 + 0.0556 = 0.5556\ldots$$

$$\boxed{x_1 \approx 0.56 \text{ (2 d.p.)}}$$

Check: the root, found by further iteration, is $0.5536$ to 4 d.p., so $0.56$ is a good second approximation.
